newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan blasts China veto, vows to assist Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan blasts China veto, vows to assist Guatemala.

text.p: Taiwan said on Saturday that China's veto of an U.N. peace-keeping mission to Guatemala was "insensible", adding its long-term friendship with its Central American ally would remain unchanged. "It's extremely insensible and unreasonable for communist China to mingle relations across the (Taiwan) Strait into a regional peace-keeping mission," Foreign Minister John Chang was quoted by state-run Central News Agency as saying.
"The move will only cause antipathy in the Central American nations," Chang said.
China vetoed a resolution late on Friday to send 155 United Nations' peacekeepers to Guatemala because of the Central American country's "erroneous position" in supporting Taiwan.
It was the first veto China had cast in nearly 25 years.

"The Guatemala authorities cannot expect to have the cooperation of China in the Security Council while taking actions to infringe upon China's sovereignty and territorial integrity," said China's U.N. ambassador Qin Huasun.

Communist China, Taiwan's archrival since a civil war split them in 1949, regards the island as a rebel province ineligible for foreign ties. It has tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in its quest to bring Taiwan under mainland rule.
But Qin added that China might reconsider if Guatemala "moves to remove the obstacles".
China took over the U.N. seat held by Taiwan in 1971.
Guatemala is one of only 30 countries, mostly poor states in Africa and Central America, which recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China governmnt instead of Beijing's communist Chinese government.
Wealthy but diplomatically isolated Taiwan gives considerable economic assistance to Guatemala.

Chang, who attended the December 29 signing of a peace treaty that ended 36 years of civil war in Guatemala, said Guatemala could count on Taiwan's full support, but denied local media reports that Taiwan intended to finance its own peace-keeping mission there.
"We will not take over matters or fundings related to (the peace-keeping mission), the Guatemala government is aware of our position," Chang said on state radio.
"However, we can help them through other channels. We can speed up existing cooperation projects so that their economy and society will have a stable development," Chang said.
"Our relationship with Guatemala will not be changed because of communist China's pressure. All cooperation projects between the two countries will be carried out faithfully and continually."
President Lee Teng-hui said on Thursday the island would "do whatever it can" to provide necessary assistance to Guatemala.
Guatemala stood equally firm on relations with Taiwan.
"We have had extremely positive relationships with Tawian for more than 40 years," said Guatemala's ambassador to Washington, Pedro Lamport.
"We are not a country which is going to change the friendship immediately. We are not going to change our friendship with Taiwan."
